tickets.title: Dormant Account Auditing
tickets.description: Performs a LEFT JOIN to find all customer records who have no active accounts in the ledger.
tasks: Performs a LEFT JOIN to find all customer records who have no active accounts in the ledger.
learning_objectives: Master relational data retrieval across multiple tables.
tickets.evaluation: `compare_result_set(actual, expected)` `check_command_used("LEFT JOIN")` **[A] Correctness (40 pts)**: 40 pts for correct user ID listing. **[B] Optimality (30 pts)**: 30 pts if indexing on `customer_id` is matched. **[C] Quality (20 pts)**: 20 pts for correct aliasing.
common_mistakes: Using a CROSS JOIN accidentally by forgetting the ON clause.
Selecting ambiguous column names without table aliases.
hints: Ensure you are joining on the correct primary and foreign keys.
Consider whether an INNER JOIN or LEFT JOIN is needed.

solution.query.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, c.email
    FROM customers c
    LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.id
    WHERE a.id IS NULL;

tickets.title: Full Transaction Reconciliation
tickets.description: Conducts a FULL OUTER JOIN to audit discrepancies between account files and transaction entries.
tasks: Conducts a FULL OUTER JOIN to audit discrepancies between account files and transaction entries.
learning_objectives: Master relational data retrieval across multiple tables.
tickets.evaluation: `compare_result_set(actual, expected)` `check_command_used("FULL OUTER JOIN")` **[A] Correctness (40 pts)**: 40 pts if missing links are captured. **[B] Optimality (30 pts)**: 30 pts for hashing-based join optimization. **[C] Quality (20 pts)**: 20 pts for explicitly naming output fields.
common_mistakes: Using a CROSS JOIN accidentally by forgetting the ON clause.
Selecting ambiguous column names without table aliases.
hints: Ensure you are joining on the correct primary and foreign keys.
Consider whether an INNER JOIN or LEFT JOIN is needed.

solution.query.sql:
SELECT a.id AS account_id, t.id AS transaction_id, t.amount
    FROM accounts a
    FULL OUTER JOIN transactions t ON t.account_id = a.id
    WHERE a.id IS NULL OR t.id IS NULL;

tickets.title: Recursive Referral Trees
tickets.description: Writes a recursive CTE to traverse ApexBank's referral structure, starting from Customer 1.
tasks: Writes a recursive CTE to traverse ApexBank's referral structure, starting from Customer 1.
learning_objectives: Understand relational database design and PostgreSQL features.
tickets.evaluation: `compare_result_set(actual, expected)` `check_command_used("WITH RECURSIVE")` **[A] Correctness (40 pts)**: 40 pts for exact tree output. **[B] Optimality (30 pts)**: 30 pts for CTE recursion speed. **[C] Quality (20 pts)**: 20 pts for structured joins within CTE limits.
common_mistakes: Forgetting semicolons at the end of statements.
Using reserved keywords as column names without quotes.
hints: Review the PostgreSQL documentation for exact syntax.
Test your queries in smaller chunks first.

solution.query.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE referral_tree AS (
      SELECT referred_id, referrer_id, 1 AS depth
      FROM referrals
      WHERE referrer_id = 1
      
      UNION ALL
      
      SELECT r.referred_id, r.referrer_id, rt.depth + 1
      FROM referrals r
      JOIN referral_tree rt ON r.referrer_id = rt.referred_id
    )
    SELECT rt.referred_id AS customer_id, c.name AS customer_name, rt.depth
    FROM referral_tree rt
    JOIN customers c ON rt.referred_id = c.id
    ORDER BY rt.depth, customer_name;
